values: VALUES: What socio-relational values (e.g., trust, flexibility, dignity, mutual care) govern the food pantry ecosystem?
Frames equitable access — able to get there when needed, regardless of rigid slots
Generic "everyone should have a ride" with no access-barrier specifics

Receiving help is conditioned on demonstrating deservingness: surveillance of recipients and an expectation of gratitude as repayment.

Include when: Lit mechanisms connecting charity to conditionality and surveillance.

Related coding: Also apply CONSTRAINTS when eligibility or deservingness requirements create a structural barrier.
The ID-card rule at the pantry.
Frames relational trust — toward a known person, not the system/vehicle
Trust framed as trust in technology reliability (code as EFF_VALUE)
community concerns — flexibility for variable need
Frames adaptability to variable/unpredictable need — household size, timing, one-time vs. recurring
Fixed scheduling described neutrally, no flexibility concern raised
Mobility as Social Service — ongoing, relational practice of equitable provisioning
Statements naming what should matter in mobility/aid — trust, dignity, mutual care, flexibility, fairness
Purely factual/logistical statements with no evaluative content
Mobility as Social Service — ongoing, relational practice of equitable provisioning

Whether a service preserves or strips dignity is a concrete, structural design property, not an unavoidable side effect of receiving help: minimizing burden, respecting autonomy, avoiding stigma.

Include when: Lit components of high-dignity service (Brenton components; Chapman journey-wide dignity), plus transcript evidence of a dignity-preserving service.
Mechanism 7: Cresswell Riol and Connelly 2023, 2025; Brenton, Tindall, Glanz, and Virudachalam 2025; Chapman et al. 2024
CARE INFRASTRUCTURE: What existing unpaid, informal networks repeatedly move food, goods, care, or information for others?
Existing informal care and distribution infrastructure

An existing, unpaid, informal person, route, or network that repeatedly moves food, goods, care, or information for others and functions as real mobility or distribution infrastructure.

Include when: A passage describes redistribution circuits, personal delivery routes for homebound neighbors, informal caregiver-as-driver arrangements, or word-of-mouth information networks that serve others.
The network is wished for or hypothetical; the activity is a one-off errand; the passage only describes personal mobility; or it names an isolated skill or resource.
CONSTRAINTS: What systemic and infrastructural constraints limit mobility and food access?
Named systemic, infrastructural, or resource limits shaping mobility — funding, geography, scheduling rigidity, staffing
General complaints with no identifiable structural cause
MEANINGS: What does mobility mean to food pantry users and stakeholders?
Mobility as Social Service — ongoing, relational practice of equitable provisioning
Statements about what mobility represents — independence, being seen, belonging, burden, care
Purely functional trip descriptions (code as PRACTICES)
AVs are not simply transportation vehicles but infrastructure
Treats the AV as infrastructure-scale — reshaping daily life/dependency long-term — vs. a one-off consumer product
Treats AV as a single ride/trip with no systemic framing
AVs are not simply transportation vehicles but infrastructure

An efficiency-led reorganization of the food system severed the residents it no longer served, and is the structural context a pantry sits inside.

Include when: Lit claims about reorganization with negative access consequences.

Related coding: Also apply EFF_VALUE and MISALIGNMENT when the passage describes efficiency-led reorganization and its exclusionary consequences.
Positive design discussion without the structural exclusion described in this definition.
PRACTICES: What socio-technical mobility practices do pantry leaders, volunteers, and clients rely on? What do they move, and how?
Mobility as Social Service — ongoing, relational practice of equitable provisioning
Concrete descriptions of how people, goods, or care actually move — who drives, what's carried, how routes/times are decided
PARTICIPATION: Who decides how mobility and food access systems are designed and run, and how do community members experience inclusion or exclusion?
Reflects the speaker/community currently has no say in how mobility tech is designed/decided
Lacking a ride rather than lacking a say (code as CONSTRAINTS)

Formal public involvement processes solicit community input through meetings, committees, or task forces, but rarely give that input binding influence over the final decision.

Include when: Lit evidence that an inclusive-sounding process reproduced exclusion or collected input without power transfer.
Community-built alternatives with real authority (COMMUNITY_BUILT / COGOVERN).

Mechanism 1: Pinski et al. 2024; Bailey et al. 2012; Karner et al. 2020; McCullough et al. 2024; van Holstein et al. 2020; Klaever et al. 2025; Hicks, Kingsley, and Isett 2025; Barendregt, Bendor, and van Eekelen 2024; Cresswell Riol and Connelly 2025; Joassart-Marcelli, Bosco, and McFadden 2026

Equity practices that claim inclusion without redistributing decision-making power (performative) versus those that do (authentic).

Include when: Lit claims distinguishing performative inclusion from real power transfer.

Related coding: Related subcode: CONSULT_NO_POWER. Use PERF_VS_AUTH when the evidence explicitly distinguishes performative inclusion from real power transfer.

People stop participating entirely after being ignored or humiliated: prior negative experiences teach them their input will not be needed.

Include when: A client's expressed doubt that speaking up matters, plus the lit mechanism.
General service distrust without a participation referent.

The default answer to who is centered is the credentialed professional, official, or researcher synthesizing data, not the resident whose mobility the system shapes.

Include when: Evidence of who a study or policy centers: who_is_centered_counts.csv, engineering policy advice authored by credentialed insiders.
Studies that do center residents or clients.
Mechanism 4: Hicks, Kingsley, and Isett 2025; Lu et al. 2020; Robles and Mallinson 2024; Zhang et al. 2024; Jeghers et al. 2024; Di Ruocco 2025; Murray et al. 2023; Shaker et al. 2023.
A moment where participation did shape a decision — including this workshop being named as a rare instance
Hypothetical "it would be nice if we were asked" (code as INPUT_PART_ABSENT)

When residents or community organizations are resourced to build their own plan, scenario, or design rather than only react to one, the result can match or outperform the agency or industry default on the sponsor's own terms.

Include when: Any lit claim that a community-authored alternative matched or beat a default, or evidence the community already runs what the formal system forbids.

Related coding: Also apply COGOVERN when community authorship has binding influence. Use CARE_INFRA only if the passage also meets its recurring unpaid care-network definition.
Consultation that collects input without influence (CONSULT_NO_POWER).
Mechanism 6: Karner et al. 2020; Gripper et al. 2022; Severs et al. 2022; Prost et al. 2018; Heitlinger et al. 2021; Baumann et al. 2018; Sörries et al. 2024; Gomes et al. 2026; Pineo et al. 2026

The community participates not as consulted public but as co-governor of the service, with binding influence over design decisions.

Include when: Lit evidence that resourced community authorship changes outcomes, and workshop conditions requiring co-production.
Mechanism 6: Karner et al. 2020; Severs et al. 2022; Tan et al. 2025
MISALIGNMENT: Where do top-down, efficiency-driven values collide with community mobility needs?
efficiency-driven values inherited from transportation engineering
Invokes efficiency logic — speed, optimized routing, throughput, scheduling precision, automation-as-improvement
Vehicle/tech mentions with no efficiency framing
efficiency-driven values inherited from transportation engineering

The Engineering/Safety literature organizes evaluation around network throughput, capacity, and automation share, with people appearing only as trip counts.

Include when: Model-level claims about capacity, penetration rate, or level of service.
Trade-offs named with riders as humans.
Mechanism 3: Lu, Tettamanti, Horcher, and Varga 2020; Park, Jang, and Ko 2024; Pimenta, Kamruzzaman, and Currie 2023
efficiency-driven values inherited from transportation engineering

Trust is measured and tuned as an individual psychological score rather than built and sustained through an ongoing relationship.

Include when: Trust-in-automation studies that model, score, or calibrate trust.

Related coding: Contrast with JUST_TRUST, which concerns relational trust.
Mechanism 2: Kraus, Scholz, Stiegemeier, and Baumann 2020; Lee and Kolodge 2020; Alkurdi and Alsaid 2025; Zoellick et al. 2019; Tan et al. 2025 (contrast)
efficiency-driven values inherited from transportation engineering

Digital food platforms judge access against an efficiency standard instead of a procedural-inclusion or recognition one.

Include when: Lit claims that platforms or systems treat access as optimization.

Related coding: Also apply JUST_ACCESS; add MISALIGNMENT when a value gap is explicit.
Digital-only pantry rules in the transcripts.
Mechanism 3: Joassart-Marcelli, Bosco, and McFadden 2026; Deener 2017
efficiency-driven values inherited from transportation engineering

Safety or acceptance is operationalized as a measurable, tunable system property, such as take-over time, perceived safety, or acceptance scores.

Include when: A study explicitly converts safety or acceptance into a system measure, model input, or optimization target.
The evidence concerns relational trust, lived access, or an unmeasured account of feeling safe.
Mechanism 3: Zhang et al. 2019; Nordhoff et al. 2020; Zoellick et al. 2019
efficiency-driven values are distant from community concerns
A named/implied value-level gap between efficiency-driven logic and community-grounded values (can be calm, reflective — not necessarily a live reaction)
A moment of confusion/pushback with no value-gap articulated (code as BREAKDOWN only)
misalignment reflects a broader pattern... without participation in shaping what the technology is for
Questions or challenges not just how the AV is designed but why it exists / who decided this was the goal
Questions about design details only (routing, hours)
PROVOCATION: How did participants react to the speculative AV provocation? What desires, needs, and concerns did it surface?
speculative AV provocation surfaced how participants reasoned about mobility
Any participant response — reasoning, imagining, questioning — directly triggered by the speculative AV concept
General mobility discussion not tied to the AV prompt
speculative AV provocation surfaced how participants reasoned about mobility
A specific live moment of resistance, confusion, redirection, or reframing in response to the AV concept — code the content of the pushback
Calm/neutral clarifying questions with no resistance or reframing
speculative AV provocation surfaced how participants reasoned about mobility

The AV field reads the same friction one thread treats as data, pedestrians testing a shuttle, stepping in front of it, pressing the emergency button, as distrust to manage, up to flagging non-compliant users to police.

Include when: Lit examples of resistance read as distrust or a problem to manage.

Related coding: Also apply MISALIGNMENT when the institutional response reveals a value-level gap.
Friction treated as a meaningful signal for design rather than as a problem to manage.
Mechanism 5: Nordhoff et al. 2020 versus Forlano and Mathew 2014
IMPLICATIONS: What concrete implications emerge from participants' reactions for reframing AV infrastructure as Mobility as Social Service?
What should change in the design or delivery of mobility services?
Synthesis prompt: draw implications from coded evidence. Link each implication to the supporting excerpts and parent codes.
MASS SYNTHESIS: What comprises Mobility as Social Service based on the findings?
What socio-relational values should be integrated into MaSS?
Synthesis prompt: Draw on VALUES and the justice-related codes to identify service principles supported by the findings.
What are meaningful service features of MaSS?
Synthesis prompt: Use MEANINGS to connect proposed service features to what mobility represents for participants.
What operational practices fit the food pantry context?
Synthesis prompt: Use PRACTICES to identify how service operations should respond to existing ways of moving people, goods, and care.
How should service design recognize and support existing care networks?
Synthesis prompt: Use CARE_INFRA to identify recurring unpaid networks the service should support.
Synthesis prompt: Use CONSTRAINTS to identify structural limits that the proposed service must address.
What are the expected outcomes of MaSS?
Synthesis prompt: Describe expected outcomes as synthesis claims linked to coded findings; distinguish anticipated outcomes from observed results.
EMERGENT: Anything relevant that does not fit the categories above.
Record the excerpt, a proposed code name and definition, and why existing codes do not fit. Review with the team before adding it to the hierarchy.

values: Codebook Notes — AV / Food Pantry Co-Design Workshops (DRAFT)
Green bands contain the category and its anchor question. Column C records the category, Column D the parent code, and Column E the subcode.
A blank subcode cell on a coding row identifies the parent definition. Blue rows contain subcodes; each subcode appears once beneath its primary parent.
Read the row-specific definition and inclusion criteria in Column F and exclusions in Column G. Secondary coding relationships are noted in Column F.
One excerpt may carry multiple codes. Apply secondary codes only when the excerpt meets their definitions.
Code identifiers and definitions are retained from the completed hierarchy. The sample's rename placeholders are not new identifiers.

Column A retains the S1, S3, and S5 links supplied in the sample. Subcodes inherit their parent's link. Blank cells indicate that no sentence ID was supplied; these mappings have not been independently verified.
CARE_INFRA replaces the former CAPABILITIES code. Apply it to existing recurring unpaid care or distribution networks serving others, not isolated skills, one-off errands, or hypothetical networks.
Values through Provocation contain the coding definitions. Implications and MaSS synthesis contain prompts for interpreting the coded findings, not additional code definitions.
Parent-code names repeated in MaSS synthesis are references to the definitions above. Expected outcomes are synthesis claims, not a new IMPLICATIONS code.

INFRA_FRAME remains in the Meanings section following the sample's grouping. Its definition concerns infrastructure-scale framing; MEANINGS separately captures what mobility represents to participants.
MISALIGNMENT captures a value-level gap; BREAKDOWN captures a live reaction such as resistance or reframing. The same excerpt may carry both.
EFF_VALUE appears in the Misalignment category following the sample. An efficiency statement alone does not establish a value gap; apply MISALIGNMENT only when its definition is met.
JUST_ACCESS, JUST_TRUST, and JUST_FLEXIBILITY are parent codes within the Values category in this layout. VALUES remains the broader evaluative code, with DIGNITY_STRUCT beneath it.
Column I preserves the literature citations from the completed codebook. Blank example cells indicate that no quote was supplied; no illustrative quotes have been invented.
Log workshop or interview ID and speaker role with every coded excerpt. Use Emergent to record candidates for team discussion.
